 Troy Aikman mourns longtime spotter David Moulton: ‘He deserved better’
 Moulton also spent two decades in Gary Danielson’s CBS booth and co-hosted Miller and Moulton in southwest Florida. 
 Credit: @troyaikman on Instagram 
 By Sam Neumann on 10/26/2026 10/26/2026 
 Less AI and more AA in your search results.
 Troy Aikman lost his most trusted confidant in the broadcast booth this weekend when David Moulton, the spotter who stood at his right shoulder for NFL telecasts since 2018, died at 59 .
 Moulton’s wife, Julie, announced his death over the weekend, revealing that he had waged a six-year fight against stage four renal cell cancer, which metastasized to his bones two years ago. Aikman, who joined Joe Buck in saluting Moulton on air during ESPN’s Monday Night Football broadcast last week , posted his tribute on social media.
 “Since 2018, David Moulton has been my right-hand man in the broadcast booth,” Aikman wrote . “What started as a professional relationship became a friendship I have cherished. David was loyal, dependable and a warrior until the very end. He deserved better. My heart breaks for his family and all who loved him. I’m grateful for the years we shared and will miss him deeply. Rest in peace big guy.”
 View this post on Instagram 
 A post shared by troy aikman (@troyaikman) 
 Aikman had his longtime broadcast partner Joe Buck — with whom he’s reportedly at odds over their diverging ESPN contract situations —  to thank for the pairing, since Buck had already spent several years working alongside Moulton on Fox’s golf coverage before recommending him for the NFL booth. According to a 2020 profile by Bryan Curtis of The Ringer , Moulton’s duties at those golf events included arming Buck with handwritten cards as each player approached the tee, and the rapport they forged there carried Moulton into Aikman’s booth on Sunday afternoons in 2018 before he added Thursday Night Football the following season.
 Moulton stood at Aikman’s right shoulder during games, and starting in 2019 he also talked to Aikman through a headset at the analyst’s request. Much of what he passed along was practical, like how many timeouts each team had left at the two-minute warning, but he also kept an eye on the matchups Aikman cared most about and raised the kind of questions fans at home were likely asking, such as why a star receiver wasn’t seeing the ball.
 On the night before this year’s Super Bowl, Aikman asked Moulton what stuck out about the game. Moulton said he was curious who Richard Sherman, the 49ers cornerback, was going to cover on third downs. Aikman liked the idea. So in the first quarter, when Moulton noticed Sherman lining up over Chiefs tight end Travis Kelce, he told Aikman, “Sherman on Kelce, Sherman on Kelce.” 
 Long before Fox came calling, Moulton held down Saturdays at CBS. His network career began by happenstance in 2003, when Gary Danielson, stranded in traffic, tuned into Moulton’s Fort Myers radio show and was impressed by his dissection of a game Danielson had called that weekend. Danielson brought him to CBS for a one-week tryout in 2006, and Moulton remained his researcher and spotter in the SEC booth from that point forward. Danielson, who doesn’t use social media, shared a statement remembering Moulton through CBS sideline reporter Jenny Dell on Sunday.
 https://t.co/i7qWbH1s1U
 — Jenny Dell (@JennyDell_) October 25, 2026 
 Radio was where most of southwest Florida knew him. Moulton co-hosted Miller and Moulton alongside Mark Miller for roughly 20 years, staying on the air until this past summer, when he stepped away to focus on his health. He also anchored sports for ABC 7 in Sarasota, served as the voice of Florida Gulf Coast University athletics, hosted for SiriusXM’s Mad Dog Sports Radio and NFL Radio, and wrote a column for the Naples Daily News and The News-Press for more than a decade.
 Moulton was quick to wave off any credit for what he contributed, telling Curtis that Aikman and Danielson watched their own film and handled somewhere between 96 and 98 percent of the work themselves. He likened his role to caddying for an elite golfer who would rank among the best in the world whether or not he was carrying the bag.
 “I’m just a helper is all I am,” Moulton told Curtis.
 But to Aikman, and countless others, he was so much more than that.
